newsitem.title: YUGOSLAVIA: Contrasting pasts of Serbia's opposition chiefs.
newsitem.headline: Contrasting pasts of Serbia's opposition chiefs.

text.p: One leader of Serbia's motley opposition movement is a blow-dried politician who championed Serbs at war, another a bearded firebrand who once formed a radical militia, and the third a devoted anti-war campaigner.

Zoran Djindjic, Vuk Draskovic and Vesna Pesic, disparate as could be, have vaulted into the international limelight at the head of eight straight weeks of peaceful demonstrations for democratic reform, taking on President Slobodan Milosevic.
Their Zajedno (Together) opposition coalition champions the ideas of liberal democracy, non-violence and a market economy.

But the three leaders lack practical governing experience and the contradictory backgrounds of two might prompt domestic critics and Western analysts to ask: Is Zajedno more qualified for power than Milosevic's autocratic Socialists?
Draskovic, a charismatic orator with shaggy black hair, flowing beard and piercing eyes, cuts the stereotypical image of a Serb nationalist warrior -- which he once was.

The 50-year-old son of Yugoslav Partisans who resisted the German occupation in World War Two, Draskovic was one of the first to espouse the cause of "Greater Serbia" -- the notion of uniting Serbs throughout the Balkans in one state.

That ultra-nationalist movement was stoked by Milosevic in 1987-91 and provoked Serb uprisings in Croatia and Bosnia which encouraged both republics to declare independence, shattering the multinational Yugoslav federation.
Draskovic assembled a rightist paramilitary force in 1991 to help the Serbian-led Yugoslav army in its eventually futile intervention to crush the secession of Croatia.
But Draskovic, whose first name means Wolf, later renounced violent nationalism and became a political foe of Milosevic, forming the opposition Serbian Renewal Movement (SPO).
Draskovic became the first Serbian opposition leader to condemn Bosnian Serbs who had overrun much of Bosnia, expelled Moslems and Croats and set siege to the capital Sarajevo.

He called on Bosnian Serbs and their then-mentor Milosevic to accept a fair and just peace accord. In response, Bosnian Serbs and Serbian state television denounced Draskovic as a traitor to the Serb nation.
He also took on a big role in demonstrations for democratic change. In 1993 Draskovic and his wife Danica were detained for weeks by security police and he was seriously beaten in jail.
Draskovic now advocates a democratic Serbia with close links to the West. But his party is a questionable mixture of republican democrats, old Serbian monarchists and ultra-nationalist Chetniks.
He is given to wild, populist rhetoric on the hustings. Diplomats and domestic critics say he can play fast and loose with the truth, depending on his audience.
By contrast Djindjic, 44, is a scrubbed, slick pragmatist -- detractors would say "opportunist" -- who studied in Germany in the 1970s and speaks fluent German.

Djindjic, who cuts a good television figure with a neatly trimmed thatch of salt-and-pepper hair and smart suits, heads the Democratic Party (DS). But he clung to Serb nationalism until only recently, after Milosevic scrapped it as untenable.

He strongly supported Serbs at war in Bosnia and paid visits to their base town Pale. He joined a feast of an ox on a spit organised by Bosnian Serb leaders in an act of defiance at the first NATO bombing of their positions in 1994.

After the 1995 Dayton peace agreement, Djindjic returned to assist the election campaign of the main Bosnian Serb party which had triggered the war and continued to seek a separate state in violation of the treaty terms.
But Djindjic has since argued that his moves were not nationalistic but patriotic. He now stands for a democratic, tolerant, corruption-free Serbia open to the world.
Pesic, 60, is a sociology professor who has campaigned for democracy and human rights for 20 years, especially after Yugoslavia started disintegrating in vicious ethnic conflict.
She gained prominence in the early 1990s as a member of the Reform Party led by ex-Yugoslav prime minister Ante Markovic.
When the Reform Party dissolved she formed the Civil Alliance. Analysts say Pesic is possibly the most trusted of the three Zajedno leaders but the least canny politician.
